lesson.title: GitOps reconciliation pull-based deployment and drift
lesson.why: Git history is not deployment state. A controller must continuously connect reviewed intent to runtime reality and report when that connection fails.
lesson.what: Trace pull-based reconciliation, controlled drift repair, and recovery ownership using an offline replica example.

concepts.name: Declared source
concepts.body: GitOps stores desired state in a versioned, reviewable source. The source must be sufficiently explicit to reproduce deployment inputs, including artifact versions. A floating image tag can change runtime bytes without a corresponding desired-state revision.

concepts.name: Pull reconciliation
concepts.body: An in-cluster or otherwise authorized controller fetches source and applies desired state. Pull-based design reduces the need for CI to hold cluster credentials, but the controller still has powerful authority and needs scoped access, trusted sources, and protected credentials.

concepts.name: Drift policy
concepts.body: Live edits create divergence from source. Automatic self-healing may revert them, while observation-only modes merely report differences. Define emergency suspension and reconciliation ownership so an operator's incident mitigation does not become a fight against an automated controller.

concepts.name: Pruning and health
concepts.body: Removing an object from desired state may trigger deletion when pruning is enabled. Synchronized manifests do not guarantee healthy applications. Separate source fetch, render, apply, and health status; a controller can successfully apply an image that crashes immediately.

e2e: A reviewed commit changes explicit desired configuration and artifact identity.
The controller fetches and renders that revision with scoped authority.
It compares live state, applies permitted changes, and handles configured pruning.
Health checks and reconciliation status reveal success or the specific blocked stage.

tasks.name: Calculate drift repair
steps: Desired replicas are three while live replicas are five after a manual edit. The difference is two excess replicas. With self-healing enabled, reconciliation returns the desired count to three; adopting five requires a reviewed source change instead of repeatedly editing live state.

tasks.name: Trace failure stages
steps: Model a valid commit that references a nonexistent image. Source fetch and manifest application succeed, but container startup fails. Record distinct controller and workload signals, and explain why a green Git merge or synchronized status does not prove the application is serving users.

tasks.name: Design emergency ownership
steps: An incident needs a temporary live replica increase. Write a controlled suspension or approved source-change sequence, assign an owner, and define how the emergency change enters Git. Include a resumption check so drift repair does not unexpectedly undo the mitigation.

tasks.name: Review deletion intent
steps: A directory rename makes a database resource disappear from rendered desired state. Determine whether pruning would delete it and require data-protection review before sync. Explain why a repository refactor can have runtime consequences even when no explicit delete command appears.

key_terms: Self-heal: automatic correction of live drift.
Sync: applying a selected desired revision.
lesson.safety: Use fictional resources; do not suspend controllers, edit live replicas, or enable pruning on a real cluster.
cleanup: Discard the drift table; no repository or cluster settings changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an emergency scale-up keeps reverting within minutes. How would you identify and safely coordinate the responsible controller?
interview_points: Check desired source and self-healing configuration.
Use an owned emergency source change or controlled suspension.
Resume reconciliation only after intended state is durable.

storyboard.title: Live edits compete with declared intent
storyboard.objective: Show drift repair and deliberate adoption.

scenes.title: Apply desired replicas
scenes.caption: Git declares three replicas.
scenes.narration: The controller reconciles the workload to the reviewed replica count.

scenes.title: Manual divergence
scenes.caption: A live scale-up is not a source change.
scenes.narration: Five live replicas diverge from three declared replicas and may be self-healed.

scenes.title: Adopt intentionally
scenes.caption: Durable intent resolves the conflict.
scenes.narration: A reviewed source update preserves the intended emergency capacity before normal reconciliation resumes.

gitops/gitops-reconciliation-pull-based-.core: GitOps reconciles explicit source, not merely Git history. Separate sync from health, coordinate emergency drift, and review pruning as a potentially destructive operation.
prerequisites: Kubernetes desired state and Git review

lesson.title: Argo CD applications sync waves and health
lesson.why: Applying all manifests together can race dependencies. Argo CD ordering helps, but health definitions and hook behavior still determine whether a release progresses safely.
lesson.what: Model an Application, synchronization phases, waves, and health gates without installing a controller.

concepts.name: Application boundary
concepts.body: An Application identifies source, destination, and synchronization policy. Projects constrain which repositories, destinations, and resource kinds are permitted. Application boundaries should reflect ownership and lifecycle rather than granting every team unrestricted deployment to every namespace.

concepts.name: Wave ordering
concepts.body: Sync waves use integer annotations to order resources within relevant phases; lower numbers run first. Negative waves can prepare prerequisites. Ordering does not create business-level atomicity, and a delay alone does not prove the previous component is functionally ready.

concepts.name: Hooks and health
concepts.body: Hooks run at defined lifecycle phases and can perform checks or migrations. Health assessments determine whether resources are ready to progress. Custom resources may need meaningful health customization; a successfully created object can still represent a broken external service.

concepts.name: Recovery semantics
concepts.body: Failed hooks or unhealthy resources can block progress. Retry policies and cleanup rules need to preserve useful evidence without accumulating stale jobs. Git reversion is often the durable recovery action; live rollback alone may be overwritten by automatic synchronization.

e2e: Argo CD resolves an Application source and checks project destination constraints.
Sync processing orders eligible resources by phase and wave.
Health and hook results gate subsequent work and expose stalled dependencies.
A corrected source or dependency allows reconciliation to resume with recorded status.

tasks.name: Sort a release plan
steps: Assign a namespace to wave -2, configuration to -1, API to 0, and verification Job to 1 within appropriate phases. Numeric order is -2,-1,0,1. Explain why a PreSync hook's phase also matters and cannot be understood by comparing wave numbers alone.

tasks.name: Design an Application boundary
steps: A team owns only a checkout namespace. Specify its approved source repository and destination in a project model. Reject a wildcard production destination merely for convenience, and explain how source review and project constraints complement rather than replace each other.

tasks.name: Diagnose a stalled wave
tasks.goal: Inspect health rather than add sleeps.
steps: Wave zero creates a custom database resource whose readiness is never assessed correctly. Identify its controller status and health contract before increasing wave delays. Describe a positive readiness condition and an explicit failed condition that would make progress meaningful.

tasks.name: Review migration hooks
steps: A migration hook writes data then times out. Require an idempotent migration identifier and preserved failure logs before retry. Compare rerunning the hook with reverting application manifests, and explain why neither action automatically reverses already committed schema or data changes.

lesson.safety: Use paper annotations and synthetic resources; do not run syncs, hooks, or migrations against a cluster.
cleanup: Discard the wave table; no Argo CD applications were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an Argo CD rollout stops at a custom resource despite successful apply. What would you inspect?
interview_points: Separate phase and wave ordering from application health.
Inspect custom-resource status and health assessment.
Repair the dependency or health contract rather than adding arbitrary delay.

storyboard.title: Wave progression depends on meaningful health
storyboard.objective: Explain a successfully applied but unhealthy dependency.

scenes.title: Apply the dependency
scenes.caption: Creation is not readiness.
scenes.narration: Argo CD creates the database resource in an earlier wave.

scenes.title: Health blocks progression
scenes.caption: The API must not race the database.
scenes.narration: An unhealthy dependency prevents the later wave from proceeding safely.

scenes.title: Confirm usable state
scenes.caption: Readiness unlocks the dependent wave.
scenes.narration: A meaningful healthy status permits the API wave to continue.

gitops/argo-cd-applications-sync-waves-a.core: Argo CD phases and waves order resources, while health gates progress. Scope Applications through projects, make hooks retry-safe, and keep recovery intent in reviewed source.

lesson.title: Flux sources reconciliation and image automation
lesson.why: Flux separates source retrieval, application, and image updates into controllers. Understanding those boundaries prevents fixing the wrong stage when a release stops moving.
lesson.what: Trace source artifacts through Kustomization or HelmRelease reconciliation and distinguish image discovery from approved deployment.

concepts.name: Source artifacts
concepts.body: Source resources such as GitRepository represent tracked content and produce artifacts for downstream controllers. Authentication, revision selection, and artifact readiness are separate concerns. A reachable Git server does not prove the requested branch or commit has been successfully fetched.

concepts.name: Applied intent
concepts.body: A Flux Kustomization builds and applies content from a source artifact, with configurable dependencies, health checks, and pruning. HelmRelease delegates chart lifecycle to the Helm controller. Controller intervals affect observation timing but do not guarantee instant application of every commit.

concepts.name: Image selection
concepts.body: Image automation can scan registries and select versions according to a policy, then update marked configuration in Git. Discovery is not deployment by itself. Mutable tags weaken reproducibility, so track immutable digests or a controlled versioning strategy and review promotion policy.

concepts.name: Troubleshooting ownership
concepts.body: Each controller exposes status and conditions for its stage. Source authentication failures, render errors, apply rejection, and workload health failures need different remedies. Avoid manually editing reconciled resources because the next successful controller pass may restore source intent.

e2e: The source controller fetches a selected revision and publishes an artifact.
A deployment controller renders and applies that artifact with configured checks.
Image automation may propose a source update under a reviewed selection policy.
The new source revision follows the same reconciliation and health path to runtime.

tasks.name: Calculate observation delay
steps: Assume source polling every two minutes and deployment polling every three minutes, with no event-triggered reconciliation. A commit just missing both checks can wait roughly five minutes plus processing. This is a conservative toy sequence, not a Flux timing guarantee; events and jitter change actual behavior.

tasks.name: Map controller responsibilities
steps: A GitRepository reports authentication failure while its Kustomization still shows the previous revision. Assign repair to source access first, not workload replicas. Explain how a stale healthy deployment can coexist with a failed source update and why both revision and health matter.

tasks.name: Review image policy
steps: A registry contains versions 1.4.2, 1.4.3, and 2.0.0. A policy restricted to compatible 1.4 releases should choose 1.4.3, not 2.0.0. Record the chosen digest and explain why an alphabetically highest tag is not a reliable semantic-version policy.

tasks.name: Design promotion authority
steps: Allow automation to update a staging branch or submit reviewed source changes, while production follows its own approved revision. Define repository write scope and branch protections. Explain why giving image automation broad production write access makes its policy part of the release authorization boundary.

key_terms: Source artifact: fetched content for reconciliation.
Image policy: rule selecting eligible image versions.
lesson.safety: Use fictional tags and polling intervals; do not connect registries or grant repository write access.
cleanup: Discard the controller diagram; no Flux resources were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, Flux reports a healthy application but never deploys new commits. Which revision and controller signals would you inspect?
interview_points: Check source readiness and fetched revision.
Compare downstream observed revision and reconciliation conditions.
Separate image discovery, Git updates, apply, and health.

storyboard.title: Source readiness precedes deployment reconciliation
storyboard.objective: Locate failures between fetch and apply.

scenes.title: Publish a revision
scenes.caption: Downstream work consumes an artifact.
scenes.narration: The source controller publishes the selected repository revision.

scenes.title: Source access fails
scenes.caption: Old healthy state may remain.
scenes.narration: A new fetch fails authentication while the previous application continues serving.

scenes.title: Resume the handoff
scenes.caption: Repair source before changing workloads.
scenes.narration: Restored source access publishes a new artifact for downstream reconciliation.

gitops/flux-sources-reconciliation-and-i.core: Flux source, deployment, and image controllers own distinct stages. Compare desired, fetched, and applied revisions; treat image-update write authority as part of release governance.

lesson.title: Helm charts values releases and rollback
lesson.why: Templates make packaging flexible but can hide environment differences and destructive changes. A release revision is useful only when its rendered resources and data effects are understood.
lesson.what: Trace chart inputs, local rendering, release history, and rollback boundaries using a fictional application chart.

concepts.name: Chart structure
concepts.body: Charts package templates, metadata, defaults, and optional dependencies. Values parameterize rendering but should remain a clear supported interface. Complex conditionals can create invalid combinations, so validate values and render representative configurations before using a live cluster.

concepts.name: Value precedence
concepts.body: User values override defaults according to Helm's merge and command precedence rules. Lists commonly replace rather than merge element-by-element. Repeated overrides can obscure the final configuration, making the rendered manifest a better review target than a collection of values files alone.

concepts.name: Release lifecycle
concepts.body: A release records an installed chart instance and its revisions. Upgrade changes rendered resources under that release identity. Hooks and custom resources can have lifecycle behavior outside ordinary expectations, so inspect them explicitly and understand namespace and ownership constraints.

concepts.name: Rollback limits
concepts.body: Rollback selects a previous release revision and attempts to restore its manifests. It cannot automatically undo external database writes or every hook side effect. CRD evolution and persistent volume behavior require separate recovery planning rather than assuming release history is a full backup.

e2e: Select a chart version and explicit environment values.
Render and validate resulting manifests before installation or upgrade.
Apply an approved release and observe readiness plus application checks.
Recover with a compatible revision or data-aware repair when rollout fails.

tasks.name: Compute effective values
steps: Defaults set replicas=2 and image.tag=1.0. A production values file sets replicas=4; a final explicit override sets replicas=3. Effective replicas are three. If the default ports list is [80,443] and an override supplies [8080], review replacement as [8080], not an assumed three-port union.

tasks.name: Design render checks
steps: For a fictional chart, inspect rendered Deployment selector labels, container port, Service targetPort, and resource requests. Explain why a syntactically valid values file can still produce a Service that routes to the wrong port or no matching Pods.

tasks.name: Diagnose an upgrade failure
steps: Compare a missing required value during rendering with a rendered image that cannot be pulled. The first blocks manifest generation; the second fails after application. Choose chart validation evidence for one and Pod events plus registry checks for the other.

tasks.name: Review rollback feasibility
steps: Revision two runs a migration hook removing a field required by revision one. Explain why a release rollback cannot recreate that field's lost contents. Propose expand-contract migration and retain a compatible rollback artifact before promising immediate recovery to operators.

key_terms: Release: installed chart instance and history.
Render: producing manifests from templates and inputs.
lesson.safety: Use paper values; do not install, upgrade, uninstall, or roll back a real Helm release.
cleanup: Discard the rendered-resource checklist; no release or chart files were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a Helm rollback restores old Pods but the application still fails. What might release history not have restored?
interview_points: Check schema changes, persistent data, and hook side effects.
Compare effective values and rendered manifests.
Verify old-code compatibility before promising rollback.

storyboard.title: Rendered manifests connect values to a release
storyboard.objective: Explain why release rollback has data limits.

scenes.title: Render the upgrade
scenes.caption: Review effective configuration.
scenes.narration: Helm combines chart inputs into the resources that an upgrade will change.

scenes.title: Data changes outlive revision
scenes.caption: History is not a database backup.
scenes.narration: A migration can alter stored data in ways a manifest rollback cannot reverse.

scenes.title: Recover compatibly
scenes.caption: Validate the old application's contract.
scenes.narration: Rollback proceeds only when persistent data remains compatible or an explicit recovery path exists.

gitops/helm-charts-values-releases-and-r.core: Review effective values and rendered manifests. Helm releases track chart revisions, not all external state; hooks, CRDs, and databases need separate lifecycle and recovery analysis.

lesson.title: Kustomize overlays patches and environment differences
lesson.why: Copying entire manifests for each environment creates silent divergence. Structured overlays make intended differences visible while preserving a shared base.
lesson.what: Model bases, overlays, patches, and generators while checking the fully rendered output for accidental scope expansion.

concepts.name: Reusable base
concepts.body: A base describes common resources without knowing every deployment environment. Overlays reference it and apply intentional changes. Keep environment-specific credentials and destinations out of the shared base so reuse does not accidentally carry production assumptions into practice.

concepts.name: Patch targeting
concepts.body: Patches modify selected objects by identity or supported selectors. A patch matching several resources can broaden a change beyond its intent. JSON patch operations depend on paths and array positions, while strategic behavior depends on supported resource schema and merge keys.

concepts.name: Transformers and generators
concepts.body: Name prefixes, namespaces, images, labels, and generated configuration reduce repetitive edits. Generated names can include content hashes to trigger references to new configuration. Verify reference rewriting for custom resources rather than assuming every arbitrary string is automatically updated.

concepts.name: Rendered review
concepts.body: The final build is the effective configuration. Review it for labels, selectors, namespaces, ports, and resource counts. Excessive overlay depth hides reasoning; favor a small set of explicit differences over a maze of inheritance and environment-specific patches.

e2e: Define a common base with stable resource identities.
An environment overlay selects targeted patches and configuration generation.
Rendering applies transformations into one effective manifest set.
Validation compares intended differences before the deployment controller applies any resources.

tasks.name: Calculate effective replicas
steps: The base API has replicas=2. A staging overlay leaves it unchanged while production patches it to five. Expected outputs are two and five, not seven. If another production patch later sets three, inspect ordering and eliminate contradictory intent rather than relying on accidental precedence.

tasks.name: Review a patch target
steps: A patch targets every Deployment with label tier=backend, matching API and worker. The requested change was API-only. Narrow the target by resource identity or a deliberate label and list the expected match count before accepting the rendered output.

tasks.name: Trace generated configuration
steps: A generated ConfigMap name includes a content hash and a Deployment references it. Change one synthetic setting and expect a new generated name plus an updated supported reference. Explain why a custom-resource field may need additional configuration for correct name rewriting.

tasks.name: Compare environment outputs
steps: Prepare a review table for image digest, replicas, namespace, and Service ports in two overlays. Permit documented replica and namespace differences while requiring the same tested image. Explain why reviewing only patch files can miss inherited or transformed values in the final manifests.

lesson.safety: Use offline manifest reasoning; do not run kubectl apply against any cluster.
cleanup: Discard the comparison table; no manifest files or resources were modified.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a production overlay changes both API and worker resources unexpectedly. How would you locate and prevent the broad patch?
interview_points: Inspect final rendered objects and patch match scope.
Narrow selectors and assert expected resource counts.
Reduce contradictory patches and document allowed environment differences.

storyboard.title: A broad patch changes more than intended
storyboard.objective: Review patch scope through rendered output.

scenes.title: Apply an overlay
scenes.caption: The selector determines scope.
scenes.narration: The overlay patch selects all resources with a shared backend label.

scenes.title: Detect unintended change
scenes.caption: Worker was not part of the request.
scenes.narration: Rendered output reveals that the worker received an API-specific change.

scenes.title: Narrow and verify
scenes.caption: Assert the expected target count.
scenes.narration: A precise target changes only the API and leaves worker configuration intact.

gitops/kustomize-overlays-patches-and-en.core: Use shared bases and explicit overlays, but review rendered output. Patch selectors define blast radius, generators need supported reference rewriting, and deep inheritance obscures intent.

lesson.title: Secrets in GitOps external secrets and encryption
lesson.why: Version control preserves history, including mistakes. Secret delivery must keep plaintext out of Git while giving workloads reliable, narrowly scoped access.
lesson.what: Compare encrypted Git content with external-secret references and plan rotation without handling any real credential.

concepts.name: Encrypted source
concepts.body: Encrypted secret files can be versioned if decryption authority is tightly controlled and the chosen tooling supports the workflow. Encryption does not remove metadata exposure or key-management duties. Losing recovery keys can make historical configuration unusable during an incident.

concepts.name: External references
concepts.body: External-secret controllers synchronize or project values from a separate secret manager under configured identity. Git stores references and policy rather than plaintext. The controller's store permissions and namespace scope determine the real blast radius of a compromised reference or controller.

concepts.name: Runtime exposure
concepts.body: Once delivered, a secret can still be exposed through Pod permissions, logs, process environments, or state artifacts. Base64 in a Kubernetes Secret is not encryption. Limit workload access and do not assume a secure repository design automatically secures the runtime.

concepts.name: Rotation and outages
concepts.body: Refresh intervals, provider availability, and application reload behavior affect rotation. Define how stale or missing values behave and allow compatibility overlap when needed. Revoking the old credential before every client has adopted the new one can create an avoidable outage.

e2e: Git records an encrypted value or a narrowly scoped external reference.
An authorized controller obtains decryption or secret-manager access.
The workload receives the value through a documented runtime delivery mechanism.
Rotation updates clients, verifies adoption, and revokes old access after a safe transition.

tasks.name: Prove encoding is reversible
steps: Run python -c "import base64; print(base64.b64encode(b'not-a-secret').decode())". Expected output is bm90LWEtc2VjcmV0. Anyone can decode that value; the example demonstrates why base64 text committed to Git is not a confidentiality control. Use no real password.

tasks.name: Compare recovery dependencies
steps: For encrypted Git, list repository access plus decryption keys. For external references, list provider availability, controller identity, and secret version access. Compare recovery complexity and centralized rotation; do not declare either model universally safer without its operational controls.

tasks.name: Diagnose stale clients
steps: A secret controller updates a Kubernetes Secret, but an application reads it from environment variables at startup. Predict that the running process still has the old value. Plan an observable rollout or supported reload and use only a nonsecret version marker for verification.

tasks.name: Design least-privilege references
steps: A team can edit a reference requesting any path from a broadly authorized store. Explain how repository write access can become secret access. Restrict store identity, namespaces, and permitted references; add policy review before allowing a new path or cross-namespace delivery.

key_terms: External reference: pointer to separately stored secret.
Decryption authority: permission to recover plaintext.
Refresh interval: cadence for synchronized values.
Rotation overlap: period accepting old and new credentials.
lesson.safety: Use only the supplied synthetic string; never retrieve, print, encrypt, or commit a real credential for practice.
cleanup: No files are created; discard the secret-flow diagram.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, Git contains only secret references yet one team reads another team's credentials. Which trust boundary failed?
interview_points: Inspect reference-edit authority and controller store permissions.
Constrain namespace and path access rather than only hiding plaintext.
Audit runtime access and rotate any actually exposed credentials.

storyboard.title: A secret reference can carry powerful read authority
storyboard.objective: Constrain controller access as well as Git content.

scenes.title: Reference instead of plaintext
scenes.caption: Git records a requested secret path.
scenes.narration: The controller uses its own identity to resolve the referenced value.

scenes.title: Overbroad store authority
scenes.caption: Hidden plaintext does not imply isolation.
scenes.narration: A malicious or mistaken path can expose another team's secret if controller access is broad.

scenes.title: Constrain both boundaries
scenes.caption: Scope references and store permissions.
scenes.narration: Namespace policy and narrow store identity prevent unauthorized cross-team resolution.

gitops/secrets-in-gitops-external-secret.core: Keep plaintext out of Git, but also constrain decryption or store authority and runtime access. Rotation depends on controller refresh and application reload, not only repository updates.
objectives: Compare encrypted and external secret delivery

lesson.title: Policy as code admission and deployment guardrails
lesson.why: Review cannot inspect every resource field forever. Automated guardrails make important constraints consistent, but bad policies can block recovery or create false confidence.
lesson.what: Connect CI policy checks with Kubernetes admission, staged enforcement, exceptions, and controller compatibility.

concepts.name: Early feedback
concepts.body: Checking rendered manifests in CI gives fast feedback before deployment. Policies can require resource limits, approved registries, or ownership labels. CI checks alone are bypassable through other write paths, so critical invariants may also require runtime admission enforcement.

concepts.name: Admission boundary
concepts.body: Admission evaluates requests before persistence. Validating controls accept or reject; mutating controls alter requests within their configured scope. Neither automatically fixes all existing objects. Evaluate updates, subresources, and controller-generated resources so enforcement covers the intended operation without surprising omissions.

concepts.name: Failure behavior
concepts.body: Webhook reachability and configured failure policy affect API availability when policy services fail. Fail-closed protects invariants but can block essential operations; fail-open preserves writes but weakens enforcement. Built-in validation options can reduce external dependencies for supported policy needs.

concepts.name: Policy lifecycle
concepts.body: Version policies, test representative allowed and denied cases, and roll out through audit or warning stages where supported. Exceptions need owner, scope, reason, and expiry. Broad permanent exemptions undermine the rule and hide which workloads still violate the intended standard.

e2e: Render desired manifests and run versioned policy tests in CI.
Admission evaluates the actual API request from any deployment path.
Violations produce actionable reasons while permitted requests are persisted.
Policy observations guide staged enforcement, bounded exceptions, and regression tests.

tasks.name: Run a local policy check
steps: Run python -c "pods=[{'name':'a','owner':'team'},{'name':'b'}]; print([p['name'] for p in pods if not p.get('owner')])". Expected output is ['b']. The missing owner is denied by this toy rule; production policy must also validate allowed owner values and resource scope.

tasks.name: Build a policy test table
steps: For an approved-image rule, list an allowed registry, a lookalike hostname, a missing image, and a permitted digest reference. State expected decisions explicitly. Explain why a string prefix check may incorrectly accept an attacker-controlled hostname that merely begins with an approved name.

tasks.name: Model webhook failure
steps: A policy webhook is unreachable during a node outage. Compare rejecting matching requests with allowing them according to failure policy. Identify critical recovery operations and design narrow tested exclusions if justified, rather than switching every policy to fail-open permanently.

tasks.name: Plan staged enforcement
steps: Start with an inventory of violations and an audit period, assign remediation owners, then enforce for the intended scope. Give a necessary exception a specific resource selector and expiry. Verify controller-generated Pods are included and review the exception before its deadline.

key_terms: Validation: accepting or rejecting a request.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic dictionaries; do not install admission webhooks or change cluster failure policies.
cleanup: The command creates no files; discard policy test fixtures after review.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a new admission rule blocks an emergency deployment. How would you preserve the invariant while restoring safe operations?
interview_points: Inspect exact denied fields and policy scope.
Use a justified narrow expiring exception only if necessary.
Test recovery paths and policy failure behavior before broad enforcement.

storyboard.title: Guardrails evaluate actual requests before persistence
storyboard.objective: Connect early checks with runtime enforcement.

scenes.title: Evaluate the request
scenes.caption: All matching write paths are checked.
scenes.narration: Admission validates the resource actually submitted to the API.

scenes.title: Explain rejection
scenes.caption: A missing owner violates the rule.
scenes.narration: The request is rejected with an actionable reason instead of creating an unmanaged workload.

scenes.title: Correct and admit
scenes.caption: Fix the contract rather than disable policy.
scenes.narration: A corrected request satisfies the tested rule and can be persisted.

gitops/policy-as-code-admission-and-depl.core: Run policies early on rendered manifests and enforce critical invariants at admission. Test scope, failure behavior, and controller compatibility; keep exceptions narrow and expiring.
